arXiv:math/0007139v1 [math.RA] 24 Jul 2000

Computing homomorphisms between holonomic DD-modules

Harrison Tsai, Uli Walther
Date: 20 July
Abstract.

Let K⊆ℂK\subseteq{\mathbb{C}} be a subfield of the complex numbers, and let DD be the ring of KK-linear differential operators on R=K[x,…,xn]R=K[x_{,}\ldots,x_{n}]. If MM and NN are holonomic left DD-modules we present an algorithm that computes explicit generators for the finite dimensional vector space HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N). This enables us to answer algorithmically whether two given holonomic modules are isomorphic. More generally, our algorithm can be used to get explicit generators for ExtDi⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Ext}^{i}_{D}(M,N) for any ii.

1. Introduction

Let D=Dn=K⟨x1,…,xn,∂1,…,∂n⟩D=D_{n}=K\langle x_{1},\dots,x_{n},\partial_{1},\dots,\partial_{n}\rangle denote the nn-th Weyl algebra over a computable subfield K⊂ℂK\subset{\mathbb{C}}, i.e. elements of KK can be represented with a finite set of data, their sums, products and quotients can be calculated in a finite number of steps, and there is a finite procedure that determines whether a given expression of elements of KK is zero or not. Let HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) denote the set of left DD-module maps between two left DD-modules MM and NN. Then HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) is a KK-vector space and can also be regarded as the solutions of MM inside NN in the following way: Given a presentation M≃Dr0/D⋅{L1,…,Lr1}M\simeq D^{r_{0}}/{D\cdot\{L_{1},\dots,L_{r_{1}}\}}, let SS denote the system of vector-valued linear partial differential equations,

S={L1∙f=⋯=Lr1∙f=0},S=\{L_{1}\bullet f=\cdots=L_{r_{1}}\bullet f=0\},

and let Sol⁡(S,N)\operatorname{Sol}(S;N) denote the NN-valued solutions f∈Nr0f\in N^{r_{0}} to SS. Then the homomorphism space HomD⁡(Dr0/D⋅{L1,…,Lr1},N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}({D^{r_{0}}}/{D\cdot\{L_{1},\dots,L_{r_{1}}\}},N) is isomorphic to the solution space Sol⁡(S,N)\operatorname{Sol}(S;N) where the identification is as follows. A homomorphism φ\varphi in HomD⁡(Dr0/D⋅{L1,…,Lr1},N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(D^{r_{0}}/D\cdot\{L_{1},\dots,L_{r_{1}}\},N) corresponds to the solution [φ⁡(e1),…,φ⁡(er0)]T∈Nr0[\varphi(e_{1}),\dots,\varphi(e_{r_{0}})]^{T}\in N^{r_{0}} of SS, while a solution f=[f1,…,fr0]T∈Nr0f=[f_{1},\dots,f_{r_{0}}]^{T}\in N^{r_{0}} of SS corresponds to the homomorphism which sends eie_{i} to fif_{i}.

If MM and NN are holonomic, then the set HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) as well as the higher derived functors ExtDi⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{i}(M,N) are finite-dimensional KK-vector spaces. In this paper, we give algorithms that compute explicit bases for HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) and ExtDi⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{i}(M,N) in this situation. Our algorithms are a refinement of algorithms given in [12], which were designed to compute the dimensions of HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) and ExtDi⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Ext}^{i}_{D}(M,N) over KK. Algebraically, our problem of computing a basis of homomorphisms is easy to describe. Namely, since a map of left DD-modules from MM to NN is uniquely determined by the images of a set of generators of MM, we must simply determine which sets of elements of NN constitute legal choices for the images of a homomorphism (of a fixed set of generators of MM). It is perhaps surprising that this is a difficult computation. One of the reasons is that HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) lacks any DD-module structure in general and is just a KK-vector space.

In recent years, one of the fundamental advances in computational DD-modules has been the development of algorithms by Oaku and Takayama [9, 10] to compute the derived restriction modules ToriD⁡(D/{x1,…,xd}⋅D,M)\operatorname{Tor}^{D}_{i}(D/\{x_{1},\dots,x_{d}\}\cdot D,M) and derived integration modules ToriD(D/{∂1,…,∂d}⋅D,M)\operatorname{Tor}^{D}_{i}(D/\{\partial_{1},\dots,\partial_{d}\}\cdot D,M) of a holonomic DD-module MM to a linear subspace x1=⋯=xd=0x_{1}=\cdots=x_{d}=0. We give a summary of these algorithms in the appendix. These algorithms have been the basis for local cohomology and de Rham cohomology algorithms [11, 17] and have been extended to algorithms for derived restriction and integration of complexes with holonomic cohomology by the second author [16].

Similarly, the algorithm of [12] to compute the dimensions of HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) and ExtDi⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Ext}^{i}_{D}(M,N) is also based on restriction by using isomorphisms of Kashiwara and Björk [1, 7]. These isomorphisms are,

(1) ExtDi⁡(M,N)≅Torn−iD⁡(ExtDn⁡(M,D),N),\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{i}(M,N)\cong\operatorname{Tor}_{n-i}^{D}(\operatorname{Ext}^{n}_{D}(M,D),N),

which turns an Ext\operatorname{Ext} computation into a Tor\operatorname{Tor} computation and

(2) TorjD(M′,N)≃TorjD2​n(D2​n/{xi−yi,∂i+δi}i=1n⋅D2​n,τ(M′)⊠N),\operatorname{Tor}_{j}^{D}(M^{\prime},N)\simeq\operatorname{Tor}_{j}^{D_{2n}}(D_{2n}/\{x_{i}-y_{i},\partial_{i}+\delta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\cdot D_{2n},\tau(M^{\prime})\boxtimes N),

which turns a Tor\operatorname{Tor} computation into a twisted restriction computation in twice as many variables (an explanation of the notation used above can be found in Section 5).

In this paper, we will obtain an algorithm for computing an explicit basis of ExtDi⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{i}(M,N) by analyzing the isomorphisms (1) and (2) and making them compatible with the restriction algorithm. In Section 2, we present a proof of isomorphism (1) adapted from [1]. In Section 3, we give an algorithm for computing HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) in the case N=K⁡[x1,…,xn]N=K[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], which is used to compute polynomial solutions of a system SS. In Section 4, we give an algorithm for the case N=K⁡[x1,…,xn]​[f−1]N=K[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}][f^{-1}], which can be used to compute rational solutions of SS. In Section 5, we give our main result, which is an algorithm to compute HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) for general holonomic modules MM, NN. In Section 6, we give a companion algorithm which computes ExtDi⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{i}(M,N) and their representation in terms of Yoneda Ext groups. In Section 7, we give an algorithm to determine whether MM and NN are isomorphic and if so to find an isomorphism. We also give an algorithm to compute the endomorphism ring EndD⁡(M)\operatorname{End}_{D}(M), the algebraic group IsoD⁡(M)\operatorname{Iso}_{D}(M), and some of their basic properties. In the appendix, we review the restriction and integration algorithms. The reader may refer to Algorithm 8.6 for a discussion of the restriction algorithm and the VV-filtration, and to Algorithm 8.8 for a discussion of the integration algorithm and the V~\tilde{V}-filtration. Finally, the algorithms described in this paper have been implemented in Macaulay 2 [6].

1.1. Notation

Throughout we shall denote the ring of polynomials K⁡[x1,…,xn]K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] by K⁡[𝒙]K[{\boldsymbol{x}}], the ring of polynomials K[∂1,…,∂n]K[\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}] by K[∂]K[{\boldsymbol{\partial}}], and the ring K[𝒙]⟨∂⟩K[{\boldsymbol{x}}]\langle{\boldsymbol{\partial}}\rangle of KK-linear differential operators on K⁡[𝒙]K[{\boldsymbol{x}}] by DD.

Let us also explain the notation we will use to write maps of left or right DD-modules. As usual, maps between finitely generated modules will be represented by matrices, but some attention has to be given to the order in which elements are multiplied due to the noncommutativity of DD. Let us denote the identity matrix of size rr by idr\operatorname{id}_{r}, and similarly the identity map on the module MM by idM\operatorname{id}_{M}.

Given an r×sr\times s matrix A=[ai​j]A=[a_{ij}] with entries in DD, we get a map of free left DD-modules,

Dr⟶⋅ADs:[ℓ1,…,ℓr]↦[ℓ1,…,ℓr]⋅A,D^{r}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\cdot A}}{{\longrightarrow}}D^{s}\hskip 7.22743pt:\hskip 7.22743pt[\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{r}]\mapsto[\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{r}]\cdot A,

where DrD^{r} and DsD^{s} are regarded as modules of row vectors, and the map is matrix multiplication. Under this convention, the composition of maps Dr⟶⋅ADsD^{r}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\cdot A}}{{\longrightarrow}}D^{s} and Ds⟶⋅BDtD^{s}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\cdot B}}{{\longrightarrow}}D^{t} is the map Dr⟶⋅A​BDtD^{r}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\cdot AB}}{{\longrightarrow}}D^{t} where A​BAB is usual matrix multiplication.

In general, suppose MM and NN are left DD-modules with presentations Dr/M0D^{r}/M_{0} and Ds/N0D^{s}/N_{0}. Then the matrix AA induces a left DD-module map between MM and NN, denoted (Dr/M0)⟶⋅A(Ds/N0)(D^{r}/M_{0})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\cdot A}}{{\longrightarrow}}(D^{s}/N_{0}), precisely when L⋅A∈N0L\cdot A\in N_{0} for all row vectors L∈M0L\in M_{0}. This condition need only be checked for a generating set of M0M_{0}. Conversely, any map of left DD-modules between MM and NN can be represented by some matrix AA in the manner above.

Now let us discuss maps of right DD-modules. The r×sr\times s matrix AA also defines a map of right DD-modules in the opposite direction,

(Ds)T⟶A⋅(Dr)T:[ℓ1′,…,ℓs′]T↦A⋅[ℓ1′,…,ℓs′]T,(D^{s})^{T}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle A\cdot}}{{\longrightarrow}}(D^{r})^{T}\hskip 7.22743pt:\hskip 7.22743pt[\ell^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\ell^{\prime}_{s}]^{T}\mapsto A\cdot[\ell^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\ell^{\prime}_{s}]^{T},

where the superscript-TT means to regard the free modules (Ds)T(D^{s})^{T} and (Dr)T(D^{r})^{T} as consisting of column vectors. This map is equivalent to the map obtained by applying HomD⁡(−,D)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(-,D) to Dr⟶⋅ADsD^{r}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\cdot A}}{{\longrightarrow}}D^{s}, thus (Ds)T(D^{s})^{T} may alternatively be regarded as the dual module HomD⁡(Ds,D)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(D^{s},D). We will suppress the superscript-TT when the context is clear. As before, the matrix AA induces a right DD-module map between right DD-modules N′=(Ds)T/N0′N^{\prime}=(D^{s})^{T}/N^{\prime}_{0} and M′=(Dr)T/M0′M^{\prime}=(D^{r})^{T}/M^{\prime}_{0} whenever A⋅L∈M0′A\cdot L\in M^{\prime}_{0} for all column vectors L∈N0′L\in N^{\prime}_{0}. We denote the map by (Ds)T/N0′⟶A⋅(Dr)T/M0′(D^{s})^{T}/N^{\prime}_{0}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle A\cdot}}{{\longrightarrow}}(D^{r})^{T}/M^{\prime}_{0}.

1.2. Left-right correspondence

The category of left DD-modules is equivalent to the category of right DD-modules, and for convenience, we will sometimes prefer to work in one category rather than the other – for instance, we will phrase all algorithms in terms of left DD-modules. In the Weyl algebra, the correspondence is given by the algebra involution

D⟶τD:xα∂β↦(−∂)βxα.D\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tau}}{{\longrightarrow}}D\hskip 7.22743pt:\hskip 7.22743ptx^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}\mapsto(-\partial)^{\beta}x^{\alpha}.

The map τ\tau is called the standard transposition or adjoint operator. Given a left DD-module Dr/M0D^{r}/M_{0}, the corresponding right DD-module is

τ⁡(DrM0):=Drτ⁡(M0),τ⁡(M0)={τ⁡(L)|L∈M0},\tau\left(\frac{D^{r}}{M_{0}}\right):=\frac{D^{r}}{\tau(M_{0})},\hskip 21.68121pt\tau(M_{0})=\{\tau(L)|L\in M_{0}\},

Similarly, given a homomorphism of left DD-modules ϕ:Dr/M0⟶Ds/N0\phi:{D^{r}}/{M_{0}}{\longrightarrow}{D^{s}}/{N_{0}} defined by right multiplication by the r×sr\times s matrix A=[ai​j]A=[a_{ij}], the corresponding homomorphism of right DD-modules τ⁡(ϕ):Dr/τ⁡(M0)⟶Ds/τ⁡(N0)\tau(\phi):{D^{r}}/{\tau(M_{0})}{\longrightarrow}{D^{s}}/{\tau(N_{0})} is defined by right multiplication by the s×rs\times r matrix τ⁡(A):=[τ⁡(ai​j)]T\tau(A):=[\tau(a_{ij})]^{T}. The map τ\tau is used similarly to go from right to left DD-modules. For more details, see [12].

2. Basic Isomorphism

The following identification, which we take from Björk [1], is our main theoretical tool to explicitly compute homomorphisms of holonomic D-modules.

Theorem 2.1.

[1] Let MM and NN be holonomic left DD-modules. Then

(3) ExtDi⁡(M,N)≅Torn−iD⁡(ExtDn⁡(M,D),N).\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{i}(M,N)\cong\operatorname{Tor}_{n-i}^{D}(\operatorname{Ext}^{n}_{D}(M,D),N).
Proof.

Since it will be useful to us later, we give the main steps of the proof here. The interesting bit of the construction is the transformation of a Hom into a tensor product. The presentation is adapted from [1]. Let X∙X^{\bullet} be a free resolution of MM, {diagram} We may assume it is of finite length by virtue of Hilbert’s syzygy theorem – namely, Schreyer’s proof and method carries over to DD (see e.g. [2]). The dual of X∙X^{\bullet} is the complex of right DD-modules, {diagram}

Since HomD⁡(Dr,D)⊗DN≃HomD⁡(Dr,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(D^{r},D)\otimes_{D}N\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(D^{r},N), we see that HomD⁡(X∙,D)⊗DN≃HomD⁡(X∙,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)\otimes_{D}N\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},N), whose cohomology groups are by definition ExtDi⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{i}(M,N). Now as is customary, replace NN by a free resolution Y∙Y^{\bullet}, which we may also take to be of finite length,

(4) {diagram}\begin{diagram}

We get the double complex HomD⁡(X∙,D)⊗DY∙\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)\otimes_{D}Y^{\bullet},

(5) {diagram}\begin{diagram}

Since the columns of the double complex are exact except for at positions in the top row, it follows that the cohomology of the total complex equals the cohomology of the complex induced on the table of E1E_{1} terms (vertical cohomologies),

(6) {diagram}\begin{diagram}

As stated earlier, these cohomology groups are ExtDi⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{i}(M,N).

On the other hand, since MM is holonomic, the complex HomD⁡(X∙,D)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D) is exact except in degree nn, where its cohomology is by definition ExtDn⁡(M,D)\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D). Hence the rows of the double complex are also exact except at positions in the nn-th column, i.e. the column containing terms (Dr−n⊗D(−))(D^{r_{-n}}\otimes_{D}(-)). It follows that the cohomology of the total complex also equals the cohomology of the complex induced on the other table of E1E_{1} terms (horizontal cohomologies), which in this case is

(7) {diagram}\begin{diagram}

By definition, the above complex has cohomology groups TorjD⁡(ExtDn⁡(M,D),N)\operatorname{Tor}_{j}^{D}(\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D),N), which establishes the identification. ∎

In the next few sections, our goal will be to compute an explicit basis of cohomology classes of the complex (6). In particular, the cohomology in degree 00 corresponds explicitly to HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) because any map ψ∈HomD⁡(Dr0,N)\psi\in\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(D^{r_{0}},N) which is in the degree 00 kernel, i.e. in

(8) {diagram}\begin{diagram}

factors through M≃Dr0/M0M\simeq D^{r_{0}}/M_{0}, hence defines a homomorphism ψ¯:M→N\overline{\psi}:M\rightarrow N. The reason why it is hard to compute these cohomology classes is that the modules HomD⁡(Dri,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(D^{r_{i}},N) in the complex (6) are left DD-modules while the maps HomD((Mi⋅),N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}((M_{i}\cdot),N) are not maps of left DD-modules. In the next few sections, we will explain how the ingredients of the proof of Theorem 2.1 can be combined with the restriction algorithm to compute the desired cohomology classes.

3. Polynomial solutions

In this section, we give an algorithm to compute HomD⁡(M,K⁡[𝐱])\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,K[{\bf x}]) for holonomic MM. This vector space is more efficiently computed by Gröbner deformations as described in [12], but we wish to discuss this special case in order to introduce the general methodology.

For N=K⁡[𝒙]N=K[{\boldsymbol{x}}], the isomorphism (3) of Theorem 2.1 specializes to

(9) ExtDi⁡(M,K⁡[𝒙])≃Torn−iD⁡(ExtDn⁡(M,D),K⁡[𝒙]).\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{i}(M,K[{\boldsymbol{x}}])\simeq\operatorname{Tor}^{D}_{n-i}(\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D),K[{\boldsymbol{x}}]).

In this case, the proof of Theorem 2.1 also leads directly to an algorithm. As a DD-module, the polynomial ring has the presentation K[𝒙]≃D/D⋅{∂1,…,∂n}K[{\boldsymbol{x}}]\simeq D/D\cdot\{\partial_{1},\dots,\partial_{n}\} and can be resolved by the Koszul complex, {diagram} The complex (7) whose cohomology computes Torn−iD⁡(ExtDn⁡(M,D),K⁡[𝒙])\operatorname{Tor}^{D}_{n-i}(\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D),K[{\boldsymbol{x}}]) then specializes to ExtDn⁡(M,D)⊗D𝒦∙\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D)\otimes_{D}{\mathcal{K}}^{\bullet} and is equivalently the derived integration complex of ExtDn⁡(M,D)\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D) in the category of right DD-modules. Oaku and Takayama’s integration algorithm can now be applied to obtain a basis of explicit cohomology classes in Hn​(ExtDn⁡(M,D)⊗D𝒦∙)≃TornD⁡(ExtDn⁡(M,D),K⁡[𝒙])H^{n}(\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D)\otimes_{D}{\mathcal{K}}^{\bullet})\simeq\operatorname{Tor}^{D}_{n}(\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D),K[{\boldsymbol{x}}]). These classes can then be transferred via the double complex (5) to cohomology classes in the complex (8), where they represent homomorphisms in HomD⁡(M,K⁡[𝒙])\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,K[{\boldsymbol{x}}]). The method and details are probably best illustrated through an example.

Example 3.1.

u=θ1+2θ2−5v=∂12−∂2u=\theta_{1}+2\theta_{2}-5\hskip 21.68121ptv=\partial_{1}^{2}-\partial_{2}

Remark 3.2.

The transfer sequence above is used to show that Tor\operatorname{Tor} is a balanced functor in Weibel [18]. A generalization of the transfer sequence is also used by the second author to compute the cup product structure for de Rham cohomology of the complement of an affine variety in [17].

From a practical standpoint, the method outlined above is not quite the final story. The detail we have left out is how Oaku and Takayama’s integration algorithm actually computes the cohomology classes of a Koszul complex such as ExtDn⁡(M,D)⊗D𝒦∙\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D)\otimes_{D}{\mathcal{K}}^{\bullet}. Their algorithm does not compute these classes directly. Rather, their method (phrased in terms of right DD-modules) is to first compute a V~\tilde{V}-strict resolution Z∙Z^{\bullet} of ExtDn⁡(M,D)\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D). Then they give a technique to compute explicitly the cohomology of Z∙⊗DK⁡[𝒙]Z^{\bullet}\otimes_{D}K[{\boldsymbol{x}}]. This complex is quasi-isomorphic to ExtDn⁡(M,D)⊗DK∙\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D)\otimes_{D}K^{\bullet}, and cohomology classes are transferred by setting up another double complex Z∙⊗D𝒦∙Z^{\bullet}\otimes_{D}{\mathcal{K}}^{\bullet}. Thus, our method as described to compute polynomial solutions requires two transfers via two double complexes.

Given the true nature of the integration algorithm, the two transfers can be collapsed into a single step. Namely, we start with HomD⁡(X∙,D)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D), {diagram} which is exact except in cohomological degree nn because MM is holonomic. We are interested in explicit cohomology classes for H0​(HomD⁡(X∙,D)⊗D𝒦⁡[𝒙])H^{0}(\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)\otimes_{D}{\mathcal{K}}[{\boldsymbol{x}}]). To obtain them, we replace HomD⁡(X∙,D)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D) with a quasi-isomorphic V~\widetilde{V}-adapted resolution E∙E^{\bullet} along with an explicit quasi-isomorphism π∙\pi_{\bullet} from E∙E^{\bullet} to HomD⁡(X∙,D)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D). That is, we make a map πn\pi_{n} from a free module (Ds−n)T(D^{s_{-n}})^{T} onto some choice of generators of ker(M−n⋅)\ker(M_{-n}\cdot), take the pre-image PP of im(M−n+1⋅)\operatorname{im}(M_{-n+1}\cdot) under πn\pi_{n}, and compute a V~\widetilde{V}-adapted resolution E∙E^{\bullet} of Ds−n/PD^{s_{-n}}/P. Schematically, {diagram} Using the integration algorithm, the cohomology classes of the top row can now be computed. In order to transfer them to HomD⁡(X∙,D)⊗D𝒦⁡[𝒙]\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)\otimes_{D}{\mathcal{K}}[{\boldsymbol{x}}], a chain map lifting πn\pi_{n} is computed and utilized as suggested by the dashed arrows. We summarize the algorithm as follows. To keep computations in terms of left DD-modules, we make use of the transposition τ\tau at various places. Applying τ\tau to the polynomial ring gives the top differential forms Ω=D/{∂1,…,∂n}=τ(K[𝒙])\Omega=D/\{\partial_{1},\dots,\partial_{n}\}=\tau(K[{\boldsymbol{x}}]).

Algorithm 3.3.

[Polynomial solutions by duality]

Input: {L1,…,Lr1}⊂Dr0\{L_{1},\dots,L_{r_{1}}\}\subset D^{r_{0}} such that M=(Dr0/D⋅{L1,…,Lr1})M=(D^{r_{0}}/D\cdot\{L_{1},\dots,L_{r_{1}}\}) is holonomic.

Example 3.4.

Let us return to the GKZ example and apply the revised algorithm. For Step 1, we have already computed a resolution X∙X^{\bullet}. Its length equals the global homological dimension. Thus for Step 2, we get a complex which is a resolution for the holonomic dual, {diagram} where u′=−(θ1+2​θ2+6)u^{\prime}=-(\theta_{1}+2\theta_{2}+6) and v′=−(∂12+∂2)v^{\prime}=-(\partial_{1}^{2}+\partial_{2}). For Step 3, it follows that we get the presentation,

τ⁡(ExtD⁡(M,D))≃D1D⋅{u′,v′}=D1D⋅{θ1+2θ2+6,∂12+∂2}\tau(\operatorname{Ext}_{D}(M,D))\simeq\frac{D^{1}}{D\cdot\{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}\}}=\frac{D^{1}}{D\cdot\{\theta_{1}+2\theta_{2}+6,\partial_{1}^{2}+\partial_{2}\}}

For Step 4, we compute the derived integration of this module. It turns out the complex τ⁡(Hom⁡(X∙,D))\tau(\operatorname{Hom}(X^{\bullet},D)) is already a V~\tilde{V}-strict resolution when taken with the shifts 0←D1​[0]←D2​[1,0]←D1​[1]←00\leftarrow D^{1}[0]\leftarrow D^{2}[1,0]\leftarrow D^{1}[1]\leftarrow 0. The integration bb-function is s−4s-4, hence according to the integration algorithm, Ω⊗Dτ⁡(Hom⁡(X∙,D))\Omega\otimes_{D}\tau(\operatorname{Hom}(X^{\bullet},D)) is quasi-isomorphic to the finite-dimensional subcomplex, {diagram} (FkF^{k} and F~k\tilde{F}^{k} are explained in the appendix.) Here, F~4​(Ω1​[−1]){\tilde{F}}^{4}(\Omega^{1}[-1]) is spanned by the 21 monomials of degree ≤5\leq 5,

{1,x1,x2,…,x15,x14​x2,x13​x22,x12​x23,x1​x24,x25},\{1,x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{1}^{5},x_{1}^{4}x_{2},x_{1}^{3}x_{2}^{2},x_{1}^{2}x_{2}^{3},x_{1}x_{2}^{4},x_{2}^{5}\},

while F~4​(Ω2​[0,−1]){\tilde{F}}^{4}(\Omega^{2}[0,-1]) is spanned by the 36 monomials

{1,x1,x2,…,x14,x13​x2,x12​x22,x1​x23,x24}⋅e1→∪{1,x1,x2,…,x15,x14​x2,x13​x22,x12​x23,x1​x24,x25}⋅e→2.\begin{array}[]{c}\{1,x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{1}^{4},x_{1}^{3}x_{2},x_{1}^{2}x_{2}^{2},x_{1}x_{2}^{3},x_{2}^{4}\}\cdot\vec{e_{1}}\ \ \ \cup\\ \phantom{xxx}\{1,x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{1}^{5},x_{1}^{4}x_{2},x_{1}^{3}x_{2}^{2},x_{1}^{2}x_{2}^{3},x_{1}x_{2}^{4},x_{2}^{5}\}\cdot\vec{e}_{2}.\end{array}

The matrix [u′−2v′]\left[\begin{subarray}{c}u^{\prime}-2\\ v^{\prime}\end{subarray}\right] induces a map between them whose kernel is spanned by the degree 5 polynomial R→1=(x15−20​x13​x2+60​x1​x22)\vec{R}_{1}=(x_{1}^{5}-20x_{1}^{3}x_{2}+60x_{1}x_{2}^{2}).

4. Rational Solutions

A duality algorithm to compute the dimensions of ExtDi⁡(M,K⁡[𝐱]​[f−1])\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{i}(M,K[{\bf x}][f^{-1}]) for holonomic MM was given in [12]. In this section, we show how to extend this algorithm so as to compute an explicit basis of HomD⁡(M,K⁡[𝐱]​[f−1])\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,K[{\bf x}][f^{-1}]). The method is essentially the same as the algorithm for polynomial solutions. Also, since any rational function solution has its poles inside the singular locus of MM, we obtain an algorithm to compute the rational solutions of MM. Finally, we remark that a different algorithm to compute rational solutions based upon Gröbner deformations was given in [12]. Here, as otherwise, we shall use N⁡[f−1]N[f^{-1}] to denote N⊗K⁡[𝐱]K⁡[𝐱]​[f−1]N\otimes_{K[{\bf x}]}K[{\bf x}][f^{-1}].

Algorithm 4.1.

(Rational solutions by duality)

Input: {L1,…,Lr1}⊂Dr0\{{L}_{1},\dots,{L}_{r_{1}}\}\subset D^{r_{0}} such that M=(Dr0/D⋅{L1,…,Lr1})M=(D^{r_{0}}/D\cdot\{{L}_{1},\dots,{L}_{r_{1}}\}) is holonomic.

Output: The rational solutions R∈K​(𝐱)r0{R}\in K({\bf x})^{r_{0}} of the system of differential equations given by Li∙R=0{L}_{i}\bullet{R}=0, i=1,…,r1i=1,\ldots,r_{1}.

  1. (1)

    Compute a polynomial ff which defines the codimension 1 component of the singular locus of MM (see e.g. [15]).

  2. (2)

    Compute a free resolution X∙X^{\bullet} of MM up to length n+1n+1. Let its part in cohomological degree −n-n be denoted: {diagram}

  3. (3)

    Form the complex τ⁡(HomD⁡(X∙,D))\tau(\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)). Its part in cohomological degree nn now looks like: {diagram}

  4. (4)

    Compute a surjection

    ϖn:Ds−n↠ker(⋅τ(M−n)),\varpi_{n}:D^{s_{-n}}\twoheadrightarrow\ker(\cdot\tau(M_{-n})),

    and find the preimage τ(P):=ϖn−1(im(⋅τ(M−n+1)))\tau(P):={\varpi_{n}}^{-1}(\operatorname{im}(\cdot\tau(M_{-n+1}))). Denote by ϖf,n\varpi_{f,n} the induced map on the localizations, Ds−n[f−1]↠ker(⋅τ(M−n))[f−1]D^{s_{-n}}[f^{-1}]\twoheadrightarrow\ker(\cdot\tau(M_{-n}))[f^{-1}].

  5. (5)

    Compute the localization of Ds−n/τ⁡(P)D^{s_{-n}}/\tau(P) at ff using the algorithm of [13]. This produces a presentation, {diagram}

  6. (6)

    Compute the derived integration module H0​((Ω⊗DLDs−n/τ⁡(Q))​[n])H^{0}((\Omega\otimes_{D}^{L}D^{s_{-n}}/\tau(Q))[n]) using Algorithm 8.8. In particular, this algorithm produces

    • (i.)

      A V~\tilde{V}-strict free resolution E∙E^{\bullet} of Ds−n/τ⁡(Q)D^{s_{-n}}/\tau(Q) of length n+1n+1,

      E∙:0←Ds−n⏟degree​n←Ds−n+1←⋯←Ds−1←Ds0⏟degree​ 0←Ds1.E^{\bullet}:0\leftarrow\underbrace{D^{s_{-n}}}_{\scriptstyle{\text{degree}\ n}}\leftarrow D^{s_{-n+1}}\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow D^{s_{-1}}\leftarrow\underbrace{D^{s_{0}}}_{\scriptstyle{\text{degree}\ 0}}\leftarrow D^{s_{1}}.
    • (ii.)

      Elements {g1,…,gk}⊂Ds0\{g_{1},\dots,g_{k}\}\subset D^{s_{0}} whose images form a basis for

      H0​((Ω⊗DLDs−nτ⁡(Q))​[n])≃H0​(Ω⊗DE∙)≃ker⁡(Ω⊗DDs−1←Ω⊗DDs0)im⁡(Ω⊗DDs0←Ω⊗DDs1)\begin{array}[]{c}H^{0}\left(\left(\Omega\otimes_{D}^{L}\frac{D^{s_{-n}}}{\tau(Q)}\right)[n]\right)\simeq H^{0}(\Omega\otimes_{D}E^{\bullet})\simeq\frac{\ker\left(\Omega\otimes_{D}D^{s_{-1}}\leftarrow\Omega\otimes_{D}D^{s_{0}}\right)}{\operatorname{im}\left(\Omega\otimes_{D}D^{s_{0}}\leftarrow\Omega\otimes_{D}D^{s_{1}}\right)}\end{array}
  7. (7)

    Let πn\pi_{n} be the composition

    ϖf,n∘φ:Ds−n→Ds−n[f−1]→ker(⋅τ(M−n))[f−1],\varpi_{f,n}\circ{\varphi}:D^{s_{-n}}\to D^{s_{-n}}[f^{-1}]\to\ker(\cdot\tau(M_{-n}))[f^{-1}],

    where φ:Ds−n⟶Ds−n​[f−1]{\varphi}:D^{s_{-n}}\longrightarrow D^{s_{-n}}[f^{-1}] is the map defined by ei↦ei⊗f−ai{e}_{i}\mapsto{e}_{i}\otimes{f^{-a_{i}}}. Lift πn\pi_{n} to a chain map π∙:E∙→HomD⁡(X∙,D)​[f−1]\pi_{\bullet}:E^{\bullet}\rightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)[f^{-1}].

  8. (8)

    Evaluate {τ⁡(π0​(g1)),…,τ⁡(π0​(gk))}⊂Dr0​[f−1]\{\tau(\pi_{0}(g_{1})),\dots,\tau(\pi_{0}(g_{k}))\}\subset D^{r_{0}}[f^{-1}] and let {R1​(𝐱),…,Rk​(𝐱)}\{{R}_{1}({\bf x}),\dots,{R}_{k}({\bf x})\} be their images in (D[f−1]/D[f−1]⋅{∂1,…,∂n})r0≃K[𝐱][f−1]r0(D[f^{-1}]/D[f^{-1}]\cdot\{\partial_{1},\dots,\partial_{n}\})^{r_{0}}\simeq K[{\bf x}][f^{-1}]^{r_{0}}.

  9. (9)

    Return {R1​(𝐱),…,Rk​(𝐱)}\{{R}_{1}({\bf x}),\dots,{R}_{k}({\bf x})\}, a basis for the rational solutions to MM.

Proof.

As explained in [12], any rational solution of MM has its poles contained inside the singular locus of MM. The proof is now essentially the same as for the polynomial case. The space of rational solutions can be identified with the 00-th cohomology of the complex (6), which specializes to

HomD⁡(X∙,D)⊗DK⁡[𝐱]​[f−1]≃HomD⁡(X∙,D)​[f−1]⊗D⁡[f−1]K⁡[𝒙]​[f−1]≃HomD(X∙,D)[f−1]⊗D⁡[f−1]D[f−1]⊗DK[𝒙]≃HomD⁡(X∙,D)​[f−1]⊗DK⁡[𝒙]\begin{array}[]{ccl}\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)\otimes_{D}K[{\bf x}][f^{-1}]&\simeq&\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)[f^{-1}]\otimes_{D[f^{-1}]}K[{\boldsymbol{x}}][f^{-1}]\\ &\simeq&\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)[f^{-1}]\otimes_{D[f^{-1}]}D[f^{-1}]\otimes_{D}K[{\boldsymbol{x}}]\\ &\simeq&\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)[f^{-1}]\otimes_{D}K[{\boldsymbol{x}}]\end{array}

Since the complex HomD⁡(X∙,D)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D) is exact except in cohomological degree nn where its cohomology is ExtDn⁡(M,D)\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D), and since localization is exact, the complex HomD⁡(X∙,D)​[f−1]\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)[f^{-1}] remains exact except in cohomological degree nn where its cohomology becomes ExtDn⁡(M,D)​[f−1]\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D)[f^{-1}]. Hence HomD⁡(X∙,D)​[f−1]⊗DK⁡[𝒙]\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)[f^{-1}]\otimes_{D}K[{\boldsymbol{x}}] computes the derived integration modules of ExtDn⁡(M,D)​[f−1]\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D)[f^{-1}] in the category of right DD-modules. The above algorithm computes cohomology classes for the derived integration modules and transfers them back to cohomology classes of HomD⁡(X∙,D)⊗DK⁡[𝐱]​[f−1]\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)\otimes_{D}K[{\bf x}][f^{-1}]. ∎

Remark 4.2.

Let us explain how the lifting of πn\pi_{n} to a chain map in Step 7 may be accomplished algorithmically. We wish to do computations in terms of DD and not D⁡[f−1]D[f^{-1}]. The idea is that localization is exact, hence any boundary in HomD⁡(X∙,D)​[f−1]\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)[f^{-1}] is the localization of a boundary in HomD⁡(X∙,D)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D). Suppose we have computed πj:Ds−j→Dr−j​[f−1]\pi_{j}:D^{s_{-j}}\rightarrow D^{r_{-j}}[f^{-1}]. Then to compute πj−1\pi_{j-1}, we first compute the images ℓi\ell_{i} of ei∈Dsj+1{e}_{i}\in D^{s_{j+1}} under Ds−j+1→Ds−j⟶πjDr−j​[f−1]D^{s_{-j+1}}\rightarrow D^{s_{-j}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi_{j}}}{{\longrightarrow}}D^{r_{-j}}[f^{-1}]. Because the existing πn,…,πj\pi_{n},\dots,\pi_{j} are the beginning of a chain map, the ℓi\ell_{i} are in the image of Dr−j+1​[f−1]→Dr−j​[f−1]D^{r_{-j+1}}[f^{-1}]\rightarrow D^{r_{-j}}[f^{-1}]. Now we use the fact that localization is exact, which means for sufficiently large mi{m_{i}}, fmi​ℓif^{m_{i}}\ell_{i} is in the image of Dr−j+1→Dr−jD^{r_{-j+1}}\rightarrow D^{r_{-j}}. To find valid mim_{i}, we can multiply ℓi\ell_{i} by successively higher powers of ff and test for membership at each step via Gröbner basis over DD. Now compute any preimage PiP_{i} of fmi​ℓif^{m_{i}}\ell_{i} in Dr−jD^{r_{-j}}. The map πj−1:Ds−j+1→Dr−j+1​[f−1]\pi_{j-1}:D^{s_{-j+1}}\rightarrow D^{r_{-j+1}}[f^{-1}] may be defined by sending ei↦1fmi​Pie_{i}\mapsto\frac{1}{f^{m_{i}}}P_{i}.

Example 4.3.

The following system of differential equations of two variables is called the Appell differential equation F1​(a,b,b′,c)F_{1}(a,b,b^{\prime},c):

θx​(θx+θy+c−1)−x⁡(θx+θy+a)​(θx+b),\displaystyle\theta_{x}(\theta_{x}+\theta_{y}+c-1)-x(\theta_{x}+\theta_{y}+a)(\theta_{x}+b),
θy​(θx+θy+c−1)−y⁡(θx+θy+a)​(θy+b′),\displaystyle\theta_{y}(\theta_{x}+\theta_{y}+c-1)-y(\theta_{x}+\theta_{y}+a)(\theta_{y}+b^{\prime}),
(x−y)∂x∂y−b′∂x+b∂y,\displaystyle(x-y)\partial_{x}\partial_{y}-b^{\prime}\partial_{x}+b\partial_{y},

where a,b,b′,ca,b,b^{\prime},c are complex parameters. In [12], the dimension of the rational solution space of F1​(2,−3,−2,5)F_{1}(2,-3,-2,5) was computed using the duality method. This system has rank 3, and its solution space is spanned by a polynomial, a rational solution with pole along xx, and a rational solution with pole along yy.

Remark 4.4.

In the next section, we give an algorithm to compute HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) for arbitrary holonomic MM and NN. Using it with N=K​[𝐱]​[f−1]N=K[{\bf x}][f^{-1}], we get a similar but computationally different duality method to compute rational solutions. The basic difference is that the algorithm of this section uses computations over DD and in principle over D⁡[f−1]D[f^{-1}], while the algorithm of the next section uses computations over D2​nD_{2n}, the Weyl algebra in twice as many variables. From the computational perspective, we believe the algorithm of this section is more efficient.

5. Holonomic solutions

In this section, we give an algorithm to compute a basis of HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) for holonomic left DD-modules MM and NN. We will use the following notation. As before, DD will denote the ring of differential operators in the variables x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n} with derivations ∂1,…,∂n\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}. Occasionally we will also write DnD_{n} or DxD_{x} for DD. In a similar fashion, DyD_{y} will stand for the ring of differential operators in the variables y1,…,yny_{1},\ldots,y_{n} with derivations δ1,…,δn\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{n}.

If XX is a DxD_{x}-module and YY a DyD_{y}-module then we denote by X⊠YX\boxtimes Y the external product of XX and YY. It equals the tensor product of XX and YY over the field KK, equipped with its natural structure as a module over D2​n=Dx⊠DyD_{2n}=D_{x}\boxtimes D_{y}, the ring of differential operators in x1,…,xn,y1,…,ynx_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n} with derivations {∂i,δj}1≤i,j≤n\{\partial_{i},\delta_{j}\}_{1\leq i,j\leq n}. In addition, let η\eta denote the algebra isomorphism,

η:D2​n⟶D2​n{xi↦12​xi−δi,∂i↦12yi+∂i,yi↦−12​xi−δi,δi↦12yi−∂i}j=1n,\eta:D_{2n}\longrightarrow D_{2n}\hskip 21.68121pt\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}x_{i}\mapsto\frac{1}{2}x_{i}-\delta_{i},&&\partial_{i}\mapsto\frac{1}{2}y_{i}+\partial_{i},\\ y_{i}\mapsto-\frac{1}{2}x_{i}-\delta_{i},&&\delta_{i}\mapsto\frac{1}{2}y_{i}-\partial_{i}\end{array}\right\}_{j=1}^{n},

and let Δ\Delta and Λ\Lambda denote the right D2​nD_{2n}-modules,

Δ:=D2​n{xi−yi,∂i+δi:1≤i≤n}⋅D2​nΛ:=D2​n𝐱​D2​n+𝐲​D2​n=η(Δ).\Delta:=\frac{D_{2n}}{\{x_{i}-y_{i},\partial_{i}+\delta_{i}:1\leq i\leq n\}\cdot D_{2n}}\hskip 21.68121pt\Lambda:=\frac{D_{2n}}{{\bf x}D_{2n}+{\bf y}D_{2n}}=\eta(\Delta).

As mentioned in the introduction, an algorithm to compute the dimensions of ExtDi⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{i}(M,N) was given in [12] based upon the isomorphisms (1) and (2):

ExtDi⁡(M,N)≅Torn−iD⁡(ExtDn⁡(M,D),N)TorjD(M′,N)≃TorjD2​n(D2​n/{xi−yi,∂i+δi}i=1n⋅D2​n,τ(M′)⊠N).\begin{array}[]{l}\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{i}(M,N)\cong\operatorname{Tor}_{n-i}^{D}(\operatorname{Ext}^{n}_{D}(M,D),N)\\ \operatorname{Tor}_{j}^{D}(M^{\prime},N)\simeq\operatorname{Tor}_{j}^{D_{2n}}(D_{2n}/\{x_{i}-y_{i},\partial_{i}+\delta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\cdot D_{2n},\tau(M^{\prime})\boxtimes N).\end{array}

Combining these isomorphisms where M′=ExtDn⁡(M,D)M^{\prime}=\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D) produces

(10) ExtDi(M,N)≃TorjD2​n(D2​n/{xi−yi,∂i+δi}i=1n⋅D2​n,τ(ExtDn(M,D))⊠N)\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{i}(M,N)\simeq\operatorname{Tor}_{j}^{D_{2n}}(D_{2n}/\{x_{i}-y_{i},\partial_{i}+\delta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\cdot D_{2n},\tau(\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D))\boxtimes N)

In order to compute HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) explicitly, we will trace the isomorphism (10). We explain how to do this step by step in the following algorithm. The motivation behind the algorithm is discussed in the proof.

Proof.

The main idea behind the algorithm is to adapt the proof of Theorem 2.1. In that proof, we saw that Tot∙⁡(Hom⁡(X∙,D)⊗DY∙)⟶p1HomD⁡(X∙,N)\operatorname{Tot}^{\bullet}(\operatorname{Hom}(X^{\bullet},D)\otimes_{D}Y^{\bullet})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p_{1}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},N) is a quasi-isomorphism. Thus it suffices to compute explicit generating classes for

H0​(Tot∙⁡(HomD⁡(X∙,D)⊗DY∙))⟶≃H0​(HomD⁡(X∙,N))≃HomD⁡(M,N).H^{0}(\operatorname{Tot}^{\bullet}(\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)\otimes_{D}Y^{\bullet}))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}H^{0}(\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},N))\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N).

Here, the double complex HomD⁡(X∙,D)⊗DY∙\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)\otimes_{D}Y^{\bullet} is in some sense easier to digest because it consists entirely of free DD-modules. However, it too only carries the structure of a complex of infinite-dimensional vector spaces, making its cohomology no easier to compute than the cohomology of HomD⁡(X∙,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},N).

Thus, we instead are led to consider the double complex τ⁡(HomD⁡(X∙,D))⊠Y∙\tau(\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D))\boxtimes Y^{\bullet} of Step 2, whose total complex T∙T^{\bullet} does carry the structure of a complex of left D2​nD_{2n}-modules. Moreover, we can get back to the original double complex by “restricting back to the diagonal”. In other words, we claim that as a double complex of vector spaces, HomD⁡(X∙,D)⊗DY∙\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)\otimes_{D}Y^{\bullet} can be naturally identified with the double complex,

Δ⊗D(τ⁡(HomD⁡(X∙,D))⊠Y∙).\Delta\otimes_{D}(\tau(\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D))\boxtimes Y^{\bullet}).

To make the identification, first note that the natural map

Dy⟶D2​n{xi−yi,∂i+δi:1≤i≤n}⋅D2​n=ΔD_{y}\longrightarrow\frac{D_{2n}}{\{x_{i}-y_{i},\partial_{i}+\delta_{i}:1\leq i\leq n\}\cdot D_{2n}}=\Delta

is an isomorphism of left DyD_{y}-modules. Let {e1,…,er}\{e_{1},\dots,e_{r}\} denote the canonical basis of a free module Dr{D}^{r}. Then an arbitrary element of Δ⊗D2​n(Dxr⊠Dys)\Delta\otimes_{D_{2n}}({D_{x}}^{r}\boxtimes{D_{y}}^{s}) can be expressed uniquely as ∑kek⊠mk\sum_{k}e_{k}\boxtimes m_{k}, where mk∈Dysm_{k}\in{D_{y}}^{s}. Similarly, an element of Dr⊗DDsD^{r}\otimes_{D}D^{s} can be expressed uniquely as ∑kek⊗mk\sum_{k}e_{k}\otimes m_{k} where mk∈Dsm_{k}\in{D}^{s}. Hence we get an isomorphic identification as DnD_{n}-modules of Δ⊗D2​n(Dxr⊠Dys)\Delta\otimes_{D_{2n}}({D_{x}}^{r}\boxtimes{D_{y}}^{s}) and Dr⊗DDsD^{r}\otimes_{D}D^{s}. In particular, this shows that the modules appearing in the double complexes are the same.

It remains to show that the maps in the double complexes can also be identified. An arbitrary vertical map of Δ⊗D2​n(τ⁡(HomD⁡(X∙,D))⊠Y∙)\Delta\otimes_{D_{2n}}(\tau(\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D))\boxtimes Y^{\bullet}) acts on an arbitrary element ∑k1⊗ek⊠mk\sum_{k}1\otimes e_{k}\boxtimes m_{k} according to, {diagram} This is exactly the way the corresponding vertical map in HomD⁡(X∙,D)⊗DY∙\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)\otimes_{D}Y^{\bullet} works on the corresponding element: {diagram}

Likewise, an arbitrary horizontal map of Δ⊗D2​n(τ⁡(HomD⁡(X∙,D))⊠Y∙)\Delta\otimes_{D_{2n}}(\tau(\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D))\boxtimes Y^{\bullet}) acts on an arbitrary element according to, {diagram} Here, we would like to re-express the image ∑k1⊗(⋅τ(Mi))(ek)⊠mk\sum_{k}1\otimes(\cdot\tau(M_{i}))(e_{k})\boxtimes m_{k} in the form ∑k1⊗ek⊠nk\sum_{k}1\otimes e_{k}\boxtimes n_{k}. To help us, note the following computation in Δ⊗D2​n(Dxr⊠Dys)\Delta\otimes_{D_{2n}}({D_{x}}^{r}\boxtimes{D_{y}}^{s}):

(1⊗xα∂βei⊠m)=1⊗∂βei⊠yαm=1⊗ei⊠(−δ)βyαm=1⊗ei⊠τ(yαδβ)m.(1\otimes x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}e_{i}\boxtimes m)=1\otimes\partial^{\beta}e_{i}\boxtimes y^{\alpha}m=1\otimes e_{i}\boxtimes(-\delta)^{\beta}y^{\alpha}m=1\otimes e_{i}\boxtimes\tau(y^{\alpha}\delta^{\beta})m.

Using it, we get that

∑k1⊗(⋅τ(Mi))(ek)⊠mk\displaystyle{\sum_{k}1\otimes(\cdot\tau(M_{i}))(e_{k})\boxtimes m_{k}} =\displaystyle= ∑k∑j1⊗τ​(Mi)j​k​ej⊠mk\displaystyle{\sum_{k}\sum_{j}1\otimes\tau(M_{i})_{jk}e_{j}\boxtimes m_{k}}
=\displaystyle= ∑k∑j1⊗ej⊠τ⁡(τ​(Mi)j​k)​mk\displaystyle{\sum_{k}\sum_{j}1\otimes e_{j}\boxtimes\tau(\tau(M_{i})_{jk})m_{k}}
=\displaystyle= ∑k∑j1⊗ej⊠(Mi)j​k​mk\displaystyle{\sum_{k}\sum_{j}1\otimes e_{j}\boxtimes(M_{i})_{jk}m_{k}}

This is exactly the way the corresponding horizontal map in HomD⁡(X∙,D)⊗DY∙\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)\otimes_{D}Y^{\bullet} works on an arbitrary element: {diagram} Thus, we have given an explicit identification of Δ⊗D(τ⁡(HomD⁡(X∙,D))⊠Y∙)\Delta\otimes_{D}(\tau(\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D))\boxtimes Y^{\bullet}) and HomD⁡(X∙,D)⊗DY∙\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)\otimes_{D}Y^{\bullet}.

The task now becomes to compute explicit cohomology classes which are a basis for H0​(Δ⊗D2​nZ∙)H^{0}(\Delta\otimes_{D_{2n}}Z^{\bullet}). To do this, we note that Z∙Z^{\bullet} is exact except in cohomological degree nn, where its cohomology is τ⁡(ExtDn⁡(M,D))⊠N\tau(\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D))\boxtimes N. This follows because τ⁡(HomD⁡(X∙,D))\tau(\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)) is exact by holonomicity except in degree nn, where its cohomology is τ⁡(ExtDn⁡(M,D))\tau(\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D)), and Y∙Y^{\bullet} is exact except in degree 00, where its cohomology is NN. In other words, the complex Δ⊗D2​nZ∙\Delta\otimes_{D_{2n}}Z^{\bullet} is in some sense a restriction complex. Namely, after applying the algebra isomorphism η\eta, we get an honest restriction complex Λ⊗η⁡(Z∙)\Lambda\otimes\eta(Z^{\bullet}) for the restriction of η⁡(τ⁡(ExtDn⁡(M,D))⊠N)\eta(\tau(\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D))\boxtimes N) to the origin (the restriction complex of a left D2​nD_{2n}-module M′M^{\prime} is by definition Λ⊗D2​nLM′\Lambda\otimes_{D_{2n}}^{L}M^{\prime}).

We can thus compute the cohomology groups of Λ⊗D2​nη⁡(Z∙)\Lambda\otimes_{D_{2n}}\eta(Z^{\bullet}) by applying the restriction algorithm. However, since we are after explicit representatives for the cohomology classes, we need to use a presentation of η⁡(τ⁡(ExtDn⁡(M,D))⊠N)\eta(\tau(\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D))\boxtimes N) which is compatible with η⁡(Z∙)\eta(Z^{\bullet}). This is the content of Step 3. Once equipped with a compatible presentation, we apply the restriction algorithm to it, which is the content of Step 4. This step produces explicit cohomology classes of Λ⊗D2​nE∙\Lambda\otimes_{D_{2n}}E^{\bullet}, where E∙E^{\bullet} is a VV-strict resolution of η⁡(τ⁡(ExtDn⁡(M,D))⊠N)\eta(\tau(\operatorname{Ext}_{D}^{n}(M,D))\boxtimes N). To then get explicit cohomology classes of Λ⊗D2​nη⁡(Z∙)\Lambda\otimes_{D_{2n}}\eta(Z^{\bullet}), we construct a chain map between E∙E^{\bullet} and η⁡(Z∙)\eta(Z^{\bullet}), which is the content of Step 5. The cohomology classes can now be transported to Λ⊗D2​nη⁡(Z∙)\Lambda\otimes_{D_{2n}}\eta(Z^{\bullet}) using the chain map, then to Δ⊗D2​nZ∙\Delta\otimes_{D_{2n}}Z^{\bullet} using η−1\eta^{-1}, then to Tot∙⁡(HomD⁡(X∙,D)⊗DY∙)\operatorname{Tot}^{\bullet}(\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},D)\otimes_{D}Y^{\bullet}) using the natural identification described earlier, and finally to the complex HomD⁡(X∙,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(X^{\bullet},N) using the natural augmentation map. These steps are all grouped together in Step 6. This completes the proof of the algorithm. ∎

Remark 5.2.

In Algorithms 3.3 and 4.1 we used the integration algorithm as the main workhorse, while in 5.1 we used restriction. As should become apparent from the appendix, these are really mirror images of each other. Rational and polynomial solutions naturally fit into the integration picture. On the other hand, most papers are written in the language of restriction.

Example 5.3.

Let M=D/D⋅(∂−1)M=D/D\cdot(\partial-1) and N=D/D⋅(∂−1)2N=D/D\cdot(\partial-1)^{2}, where DD is the first Weyl algebra. 7. Isomorphism Classes of DD-modules

In this section, we give an algorithm to determine if two holonomic DD-modules MM and NN are isomorphic and if so to produce an explicit isomorphism. For M=NM=N, we also give an algorithm to find all isomorphisms from MM to MM and mention some well-known applications of the endomorphism ring EndD⁡(M)\operatorname{End}_{D}(M). Here, EndD⁡(M)\operatorname{End}_{D}(M) denotes the space of endomorphisms of a DD-module M=DrM/IMM=D^{r_{M}}/I_{M}, where endomorphism means DD-linear maps from MM to MM. Similarly, IsoD⁡(M)\operatorname{Iso}_{D}(M) denotes the units of the ring EndD⁡(M)\operatorname{End}_{D}(M).

If holonomic MM and NN are isomorphic, then HomD⁡(M,N)≃EndD⁡(M)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N)\simeq\operatorname{End}_{D}(M) is a finite-dimensional KK-algebra. In the theory of finite dimensional KK-algebras, the Jacobson radical JJ is the intersection of all maximal left ideals of EE, and it has the property that the quotient E/JE/J is a semi-simple KK-algebra. By the Wedderburn-Artin theorem, a semi-simple algebra is isomorphic to a direct product of matrix rings over division algebras, and hence by taking the algebraic closure, we find that E/J⊗KK¯E/J\otimes_{K}\overline{K} is isomorphic to a direct product of matrix rings over the field K¯\overline{K}. One consequence of this decomposition is that the non-units of E/J⊗KK¯E/J\otimes_{K}\overline{K} form a determinantal hypersurface. In particular, the units of E/J⊗KK¯E/J\otimes_{K}\overline{K} form a Zariski open set, and hence the units of E/JE/J also form a Zariski open set. Moreover, units and non-units respect the Jacobson radical in the sense that if jj is in the Jacobson radical of EE and if uu is a unit of EE then u+ju+j is also a unit, and similarly, if nn is not a unit of EE then n+jn+j is not a unit. We can thus conclude the following lemma.

Lemma 7.1.

Let MM be a holonomic DD-module. Then the space of DD-linear isomorphisms IsoD⁡(M)\operatorname{Iso}_{D}(M) from MM to itself is open in EndD⁡(M)\operatorname{End}_{D}(M) under the Zariski topology.

The lemma says that if holonomic MM and NN are isomorphic then most maps from MM to NN are isomorphisms. We now give an algorithm to determine if MM and NN are isomorphic based on Algorithm 5.1 and Lemma 7.1.

Algorithm 7.2.

(Is MM isomorphic to NN?)

Input: presentations M≃DmM/D⋅{P1,…,Pa}M\simeq D^{m_{M}}/D\cdot\{P_{1},\dots,P_{a}\} and N≃DmN/D⋅{Q1,…,Qb}N\simeq D^{m_{N}}/D\cdot\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{b}\} of left holonomic DD-modules.

Output: “No” if M≄NM\not\simeq N; and “Yes” together with an isomorphism ι:M→N\iota:M\to N if M≃NM\simeq N.

  1. (1)

    Compute bases {s1,…,sσ}\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{\sigma}\} and {t1,…,tτ}\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{\tau}\} for the vector spaces V=HomD⁡(M,N)V=\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) and W=HomD⁡(N,M)W=\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(N,M) using Algorithm 5.1, where sis_{i} and tjt_{j} are respectively mM×mMm_{M}\times m_{M} and mN×mNm_{N}\times m_{N} matrices with entries in DD representing homomorphisms by right multiplication. Recall that we view DmMD^{m_{M}} and DmND^{m_{N}} as consisting of row vectors. If σ≠τ\sigma\neq\tau, return “No” and exit.

  2. (2)

    Introduce new indeterminates {μi}1τ\{\mu_{i}\}_{1}^{\tau} and {ν}1τ\{\nu\}_{1}^{\tau}, and form the “generic homomorphisms” ∑iμi​si∈HomD⁡(M,N)\sum_{i}\mu_{i}s_{i}\in\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) and ∑jνj​tj∈HomD⁡(N,M)\sum_{j}\nu_{j}t_{j}\in\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(N,M). Then the compositions ∑i,jμi​νj​si⋅tj:M→N→M\sum_{i,j}\mu_{i}\nu_{j}s_{i}\cdot t_{j}:M\to N\to M and ∑i,jμi​νj​tj⋅si:N→M→N\sum_{i,j}\mu_{i}\nu_{j}t_{j}\cdot s_{i}:N\to M\to N are respectively mM×mMm_{M}\times m_{M} and mN×mNm_{N}\times m_{N}-matrices with entries in D⁡[μ1,…,μmM,ν1,…,νmN]D[\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{m_{M}},\nu_{1},\dots,\nu_{m_{N}}].

  3. (3)

    Reduce the rows of the matrix ∑i,jμi​νj​si⋅tj−idmM\sum_{i,j}\mu_{i}\nu_{j}s_{i}\cdot t_{j}-\operatorname{id}_{m_{M}} modulo a Gröbner basis for D⋅{P1,…,Pa}⊂DmMD\cdot\{P_{1},\dots,P_{a}\}\subset D^{m_{M}}. Force this reduction to be zero by setting the coefficients (which are inhomogeneous bilinear polynomials in μi\mu_{i}, νj\nu_{j}) of every standard monomial in every entry to be zero. Collect these relations in the ideal IM⊂K⁡[μ1,…,μmM,ν1,…,νmN]I_{M}\subset K[\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{m_{M}},\nu_{1},\dots,\nu_{m_{N}}]

  4. (4)

    Similarly, reduce the rows of the matrix ∑i,jμi​νj​tj⋅si−idmN\sum_{i,j}\mu_{i}\nu_{j}t_{j}\cdot s_{i}-\operatorname{id}_{m_{N}} modulo a Gröbner basis for D⋅{Q1,…,Qb}⊂DmND\cdot\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{b}\}\subset D^{m_{N}}. Force this reduction to be zero by setting the coefficients of every standard monomial in every entry to be zero, and collect these relations in the ideal IN⊂K⁡[𝝁,𝝂]I_{N}\subset K[{\boldsymbol{\mu}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}].

  5. (5)

    Put I⁡(V,W)=IM+IN⊂K⁡[𝝁,𝝂]I(V,W)=I_{M}+I_{N}\subset K[{\boldsymbol{\mu}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}]. If I⁡(V,W)I(V,W) contains a unit, return “No” and exit.

  6. (6)

    Otherwise compute an isomorphism ∑i=1τki​si\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}k_{i}s_{i} in HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) by finding the first τ\tau coordinates of any point in the zero locus of I⁡(V,W)I(V,W). For instance, we can do this by inductively finding ki∈Kk_{i}\in K for each ii from 11 to τ\tau such that I⁡(V,W)+(μ1−k1,…,μi−ki)I(V,W)+(\mu_{1}-k_{1},\dots,\mu_{i}-k_{i}) is a proper ideal. At each step ii, this can be accomplished by trying different numbers for kik_{i} until a suitable choice is found.

  7. (7)

    Return “Yes” and the isomorphism (∑i=1τki​si):M→N(\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}k_{i}s_{i}):M\rightarrow N.

Remark 7.3.

Algorithm 7.2 can also be modified to detect whether MM is a direct summand of NN. Namely MM is a direct summand of NN if and only if the ideal IMI_{M} of step 3 is not the unit ideal. Similarly NN is a direct summand of MM if and only if the ideal INI_{N} of step 4 is not the unit ideal.

Proof.

Reduction of the generic matrix ∑i,jμi​νj​si⋅tj−idmM\sum_{i,j}\mu_{i}\nu_{j}s_{i}\cdot t_{j}-\operatorname{id}_{m_{M}} modulo D⋅{P1,…,Pa}D\cdot\{P_{1},\dots,P_{a}\} in step 3 leads to a generic remainder which depends on the parameters μi,νj\mu_{i},\nu_{j}. Moreover, since a Gröbner basis of D⋅{P1,…,Pa}D\cdot\{P_{1},\dots,P_{a}\} is parameter-free, this generic remainder has the property that its specialization to a fixed choice of parameters μi=ai,νj=bj\mu_{i}=a_{i},\nu_{j}=b_{j} gives the remainder of ∑i,jai​bj​si⋅tj−idmM\sum_{i,j}a_{i}b_{j}s_{i}\cdot t_{j}-\operatorname{id}_{m_{M}} modulo D⋅{P1,…,Pa}D\cdot\{P_{1},\dots,P_{a}\}. Thus setting the remainder to zero in step 3 corresponds to deriving conditions on the parameters μi,νj\mu_{i},\nu_{j} which makes the endomorphism given by ∑i,jμi​νj​si⋅tj\sum_{i,j}\mu_{i}\nu_{j}s_{i}\cdot t_{j} equal to the identity on MM. This is possible if and only if MM is a direct summand of NN. The analogous statement holds for reduction of ∑i,jμi​νj​tj⋅si−idmN\sum_{i,j}\mu_{i}\nu_{j}t_{j}\cdot s_{i}-\operatorname{id}_{m_{N}} modulo D⋅{Q1,…,Qb}D\cdot\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{b}\} and setting its resulting remainder to zero. Here, setting a remainder to zero is equivalent to the vanishing of the coefficients of its standard monomials, and we collect these vanishing conditions in the ideal I⁡(V,W)I(V,W) of K⁡[𝝁,𝝂]K[{\boldsymbol{\mu}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}].

Now a linear combination ∑iai​si:M→N\sum_{i}a_{i}s_{i}:M\rightarrow N is an isomorphism with inverse ∑bj​tj:N→M\sum b_{j}t_{j}:N\rightarrow M if and only if the composition ∑i,jai​bj​si⋅tj\sum_{i,j}a_{i}b_{j}s_{i}\cdot t_{j} is congruent to idmM\operatorname{id}_{m_{M}} modulo D⋅{P1,…,Pa}D\cdot\{P_{1},\dots,P_{a}\} and the opposite composition ∑i,jai​bj​tj⋅si\sum_{i,j}a_{i}b_{j}t_{j}\cdot s_{i} is congruent to idmN\operatorname{id}_{m_{N}} modulo D⋅{Q1,…,Qb}D\cdot\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{b}\}. Thus the common zeroes (a1,…,aτ,b1,…,bτ)(a_{1},\dots,a_{\tau},b_{1},\dots,b_{\tau}) of I⁡(V,W)I(V,W) correspond to isomorphisms ∑iai​si\sum_{i}a_{i}s_{i} and their inverses ∑jbj​tj\sum_{j}b_{j}t_{j}. In particular, if I⁡(V,W)I(V,W) is the entire ring, which we detect by searching for 11 in a Gröbner basis of I⁡(V,W)I(V,W), then there are no isomorphisms.

On the other hand if I⁡(V,W)I(V,W) is proper, then MM and NN are isomorphic and we obtain an explicit isomorphism from finding any common solution of I⁡(V,W)I(V,W). By Lemma 7.1, the invertible homomorphisms from MM to NN are Zariski dense in the vector space HomD⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N). Hence, a common solution can be explicitly found by by intersecting the zero locus of I⁡(V,W)I(V,W) with a suitable number of generic hyperplanes {μ=ki}\{\mu=k_{i}\}. Because of denseness, each of these hyperplanes can be found in a finite number of steps. In other words, if I⁡(V,W)+⟨μ1−k1,…,μ−ki−1⟩I(V,W)+\langle\mu_{1}-k_{1},\dots,\mu-k_{i-1}\rangle is proper, then there are only finitely many kik_{i} for which the sum I⁡(V,W)+⟨μ1−k1,…,μ−ki⟩I(V,W)+\langle\mu_{1}-k_{1},\dots,\mu-k_{i}\rangle is the unit ideal. ∎

Remark 7.4.

Once we have specialized the μi\mu_{i} in a common solution of I⁡(V,W)I(V,W), then the νj\nu_{j} are determined because of the bilinear nature of the relations (which gives linear relations for the νj\nu_{j} once all μi\mu_{i} are chosen). This also means that if there is any solution, then the μi\mu_{i} are rational functions in the νj\nu_{j} and vice versa. In particular, if ϕ∈HomD⁡(M,N)\phi\in\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) is defined over the field KK then ϕ−1\phi^{-1} is defined over KK as well and no field extensions are required. We now give two simple examples, one where MM and NN are isomorphic, and one where they are not.

We see that we have to avoid μ4=0\mu_{4}=0 but otherwise have complete choice.

Example 7.6.

Let n=1n=1, M=D/D⋅∂2M=D/D\cdot\partial^{2}, and N=D/D⋅∂N=D/D\cdot\partial. One checks that V=HomD⁡(N,M)V=\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(N,M) is generated by t1=⋅(∂)t_{1}=\cdot(\partial) and t2=⋅(x∂−1)t_{2}=\cdot(x\partial-1) while W=HomD⁡(M,N)W=\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,N) is generated by s1=⋅(1)s_{1}=\cdot(1) and s2=⋅(x)s_{2}=\cdot(x). The sum ∑μi​νj​si⋅tj\sum\mu_{i}\nu_{j}s_{i}\cdot t_{j} takes the form

μ2ν2x2∂+(μ1ν2+μ2ν1)x∂+μ1ν1∂−(μ1ν2+μ2ν2).\displaystyle\mu_{2}\nu_{2}x^{2}\partial+(\mu_{1}\nu_{2}+\mu_{2}\nu_{1})x\partial+\mu_{1}\nu_{1}\partial-(\mu_{1}\nu_{2}+\mu_{2}\nu_{2}).

Modulo D⋅∂D\cdot\partial we want this to be 1, so we get the relation

μ2​ν1−μ1​ν2=1.\displaystyle\mu_{2}\nu_{1}-\mu_{1}\nu_{2}=1.

We note that this equation has plenty of solutions, which means that MM can be realized as a summand of NN. On the other hand, the sum ∑μi​νj​tj⋅si\sum\mu_{i}\nu_{j}t_{j}\cdot s_{i} takes the form

μ1ν1∂+(μ1ν2+μ2ν1)x∂−μ1ν2−μ2ν2x+μ2ν2x2∂.\displaystyle\mu_{1}\nu_{1}\partial+(\mu_{1}\nu_{2}+\mu_{2}\nu_{1})x\partial-\mu_{1}\nu_{2}-\mu_{2}\nu_{2}x+\mu_{2}\nu_{2}x^{2}\partial.

Modulo D⋅∂2D\cdot\partial^{2} we want this to be 1, so we get the relations

−μ1​ν2\displaystyle-\mu_{1}\nu_{2} =\displaystyle= 1,\displaystyle 1,
μ1​ν1\displaystyle\mu_{1}\nu_{1} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0,
μ1​ν2+μ2​ν1\displaystyle\mu_{1}\nu_{2}+\mu_{2}\nu_{1} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0,
μ2​ν2\displaystyle\mu_{2}\nu_{2} =\displaystyle= 0.\displaystyle 0.

Putting all the equations together, we obtain the unit ideal, and hence MM and NN are not isomorphic.

For MM and NN isomorphic, we now give a method to find all possible isomorphisms, that is we study the units IsoD⁡(M)\operatorname{Iso}_{D}(M) in the endomorphism ring V=EndD⁡(M)V=\operatorname{End}_{D}(M).

Lemma 7.7.

The isomorphism set IsoD⁡(M)\operatorname{Iso}_{D}(M) is a smooth affine variety which is connected if KK is algebraically closed.

Proof.

As we have seen, IsoD⁡(M)\operatorname{Iso}_{D}(M) is isomorphic to the nonempty affine variety Var⁡(M)=Var⁡(I⁡(V,V))\operatorname{Var}(M)=\operatorname{Var}(I(V,V)) defined in the variables μi,νj\mu_{i},\nu_{j}. Here, a point of Var⁡(M)\operatorname{Var}(M) with coordinates (μ1,…,μτ,ν1,…,ντ)(\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{\tau},\nu_{1},\dots,\nu_{\tau}) corresponds to the isomorphism ∑i=1τμi​si\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}\mu_{i}s_{i}. Now any isomorphism ϕ:M→M\phi:M\to M induces an isomorphism from the variety to itself, sending (μ,ν)(\mu,\nu) to (μ′,ν′)(\mu^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}) where ∑μi​si∘ϕ=∑μi′​si\sum\mu_{i}s_{i}\circ\phi=\sum\mu_{i}^{\prime}s_{i}. This action is regular in ϕ\phi (since we showed μ\mu is rational in ν\nu), and transitive since ψ∈HomD⁡(M,M)\psi\in\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(M,M) equals (ψ∘ϕ−1)∘ϕ(\psi\circ\phi^{-1})\circ\phi. It follows that Var⁡(M)\operatorname{Var}(M) is a smooth variety because it is a homogeneous space over itself via a transitive action. As we have seen in Lemma 7.1, Iso⁡(M)\operatorname{Iso}(M) is Zariski open in EndD⁡(M)\operatorname{End}_{D}(M) (which is an affine space and therefore normal) and hence connected if KK is algebraically closed. ∎

Since the isomorphisms IsoD⁡(M)\operatorname{Iso}_{D}(M) are Zariski open in EndD⁡(M)\operatorname{End}_{D}(M), one can ask for a method to compute the equations defining the complementary closed set of non-isomorphisms.

Definition 7.8.

The ideal in K⁡[ν]K[\nu] that determines the closed set EndD⁡(M)∖IsoD⁡(M)\operatorname{End}_{D}(M)\setminus\operatorname{Iso}_{D}(M) of non-isomorphisms of MM is called Δ⁡(M)\Delta(M), the defect ideal.

Algorithm 7.9.

(Computing the defect ideal)

Input: Generators for a holonomic DD-module MM.

Output: The defect ideal Δ⁡(M)\Delta(M) defining the non-isomorphisms of EndD⁡(M)\operatorname{End}_{D}(M).

  1. (1)

    Perform Steps 1 through 4 of Algorithm 7.2 with M=NM=N as input to obtain the ideal I⁡(V,V)⊂K⁡[{μi}∪{νj}]I(V,V)\subset K[\{\mu_{i}\}\cup\{\nu_{j}\}].

  2. (2)

    Regard each of the ζ\zeta generators of I⁡(V,V)I(V,V) as a linear inhomogeneous equation in the variables μi\mu_{i} with coefficients involving νj\nu_{j} as parameters, and collect all these equations in a single matrix equation A⋅μ=bA\cdot\mu=b, A∈K​[ν]ζ×τA\in K[\nu]^{\zeta\times\tau}.

  3. (3)

    Compute all τ×τ\tau\times\tau minors of AA and collect them in an ideal Δ⁡(M)⊂K⁡[ν]\Delta(M)\subset K[\nu].

  4. (4)

    Return Δ⁡(M)\Delta(M).

Proof.

A point ν\nu corresponds to an isomorphism with inverse μ\mu if and only if the system A⋅μ=bA\cdot\mu=b has exactly one solution for μ\mu. This is equivalent to the ζ×τ\zeta\times\tau matrix AA having rank τ\tau and the augmented matrix (A|b)(A|b) also having rank τ\tau. The matrix AA will have rank τ\tau if and only if any one of its τ×τ\tau\times\tau minors is nonzero. Similarly, the augmented matrix (A|b)(A|b) will also have rank τ\tau if in addition all (τ+1)×(τ+1)(\tau+1)\times(\tau+1) minors vanish. We claim that each (τ+1)×(τ+1)(\tau+1)\times(\tau+1) minor of (A|b)(A|b) must actually be identically zero. Otherwise it would impose an algebraic condition which must be satisfied by the isomorphisms in the coordinates ν\nu of EndD⁡(M)\operatorname{End}_{D}(M). But this cannot happen since the isomorphisms are an open set by Lemma 7.1. Thus we have shown that the space of non-isomorphisms ν\nu is defined by the equations obtained from the vanishing of all τ×τ\tau\times\tau minors of AA. ∎

Remark 7.10.

In Lemma 7.1, we saw that modulo the Jacobson radical, which is a linear subspace, then EndD⁡(M)\operatorname{End}_{D}(M) is the product of simple KK-algebras. Moreover when KK is algebraically closed, then a simple KK-algebra is a matrix algebra. It follows that in an algebraic closure of KK, the radical of Δ⁡(M)\Delta(M) is generated by linear forms corresponding to the Jacobson radical and a single determinant which is the product of the determinants of the matrix algebras. However, we have not yet understood what happens when the field of input KK is not algebraically closed. Optimistically, we hope that Algorithm 7.9 produces an ideal Δ⁡(M)\Delta(M) whose radical over KK is also generated by linear forms and a single determinant. The following example shows at least that Δ⁡(M)\Delta(M) might not be radical.

Example 7.11.

Let us look at our Example 7.5. There the system of equations {−μ1ν4+μ3ν3=1,−μ2ν4−μ3ν4−μ4ν3=0,μ1(ν2+ν3)+μ3ν1=0,μ1ν4+μ2(ν2+ν3)+μ3ν2−μ4ν1=0}\{-\mu_{1}\nu_{4}+\mu_{3}\nu_{3}=1,-\mu_{2}\nu_{4}-\mu_{3}\nu_{4}-\mu_{4}\nu_{3}=0,\mu_{1}(\nu_{2}+\nu_{3})+\mu_{3}\nu_{1}=0,\mu_{1}\nu_{4}+\mu_{2}(\nu_{2}+\nu_{3})+\mu_{3}\nu_{2}-\mu_{4}\nu_{1}=0\} can be rewritten in the form A⋅μ=bA\cdot\mu=b as,

(−ν4ν3−ν4−ν4−ν3ν2+ν3ν1ν4ν2+ν3ν2−ν1)​(μ1μ2μ3μ4)=(1000)\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccccccc}-\nu_{4}&&\nu_{3}&\\ &-\nu_{4}&-\nu_{4}&-\nu_{3}\\ \nu_{2}+\nu_{3}&&\nu_{1}&\\ \nu_{4}&\nu_{2}+\nu_{3}&\nu_{2}&-\nu_{1}\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\mu_{1}\\ \mu_{2}\\ \mu_{3}\\ \mu_{4}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ 0\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right)

In order to assure that AA has full rank we need the determinant

Δ⁡(M)=ν22​ν32+2​ν2​ν33+ν34+2​ν1​ν2​ν3​ν4+2​ν1​ν32​ν4+ν12​ν42\Delta(M)=\nu_{2}^{2}\nu_{3}^{2}+2\nu_{2}\nu_{3}^{3}+\nu_{3}^{4}+2\nu_{1}\nu_{2}\nu_{3}\nu_{4}+2\nu_{1}\nu_{3}^{2}\nu_{4}+\nu_{1}^{2}\nu_{4}^{2}

to be nonzero. We conclude that the locus of not invertible morphisms is given by the vanishing of the determinant of Δ⁡(M)\Delta(M). Note also that Δ⁡(M)=(ν2​ν3+ν32+ν1​ν4)2\Delta(M)=(\nu_{2}\nu_{3}+\nu_{3}^{2}+\nu_{1}\nu_{4})^{2} which in particular is not square free.

We end by discussing the endomorphism ring E=EndD⁡(M)E=\operatorname{End}_{D}(M).

Remark 7.12.

A well-known application of E=EndD⁡(M)E=\operatorname{End}_{D}(M) is towards decompositions of MM. By the Krull-Schmidt-Azumaya theorem, a DD-module MM has a decomposition into a direct sum of indecomposable submodules (meaning that they cannot be further decomposed into a direct sum of nonzero submodules), and any such decomposition is unique up to re-ordering and isomorphism (see e.g. [8, Theorem 19.21]). There is a bijective correspondence between (1) the decompositions of MM into a direct sum of submodules and (2) the decompositions of the identity element 1=e1+⋯+es1=e_{1}+\cdots+e_{s} of EE into pairwise orthogonal idempotents [3, Theorem 1.7.2]. The correspondence is gotten by taking a set of orthogonal idempotents {e1,…,es}\{e_{1},\dots,e_{s}\} and producing the decomposition M=e1⋅M⊕⋯⊕es⋅MM=e_{1}\cdot M\oplus\cdots\oplus e_{s}\cdot M. Thus, an algorithm which produces a full set of orthogonal idempotents for the KK-algebra EndD⁡(M)\operatorname{End}_{D}(M) combined with Algorithm 5.1 would give a method to decompose holonomic DD-modules into indecomposables.

Computation in finite-dimensional KK-algebras EE has recently been an area of active research. When KK is a number field, early work of Friedl and Ronyai provides polynomial-time algorithms to decompose EE into simple algebras if EE is semi-simple and to find the radical of EE in general [5]. When K=ℂK={\mathbb{C}}, Eberly has given Las Vegas polynomial time algorithms to find the decomposition of a simple algebra as a full matrix ring [4]. We should also mention that the radical of EE is independent of field extension of KK while the decomposition into simple algebras depends upon the field KK. Thus if we are willing to use K=ℂK={\mathbb{C}}, then a full set of orthogonal idempotents can indeed be algorithmically computed.

Let us also describe another method based on computational algebraic geometry to obtain information on the invariants did_{i} in the decomposition

E/Jac(E)⊗KK¯=∏1dEndK¯(K¯di)E/\operatorname{Jac}(E)\otimes_{K}\bar{K}=\prod_{1}^{d}\operatorname{End}_{\bar{K}}(\bar{K}^{d_{i}})

where K¯\bar{K} denotes the algebraic closure of KK. We will compute the de Rham cohomology groups of the complement of Var⁡(Δ⁡(M))\operatorname{Var}(\Delta(M)) in EndD⁡(M)=ℂτ=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[ν])\operatorname{End}_{D}(M)={\mathbb{C}}^{\tau}=\operatorname{Spec}({\mathbb{C}}[\nu]) using the algorithm developed by the second author in [16]. This algorithm will in some sense allow us to pretend that KK is already algebraically closed. Namely, the algorithm can be used on input defined over any computable subfield of the complex numbers, but always computes dimℂ(Hd​R∙​(ℂn∖Y,ℂ))\dim_{\mathbb{C}}(H^{\bullet}_{dR}({\mathbb{C}}^{n}\setminus Y,{\mathbb{C}})). What we now need is a method that enables us to sort out the did_{i} from the Betti numbers of ℂτ∖Var⁡(Δ⁡(M)){\mathbb{C}}^{\tau}\setminus\operatorname{Var}(\Delta(M)).

Consider E⊗KℂE\otimes_{K}{\mathbb{C}}. As we have shown, its units are (homotopy equivalent to) the units of a product of the form ∏i=1dEndℂ⁡(ℂdi)\prod_{i=1}^{d}\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{C}}({\mathbb{C}}^{d_{i}}). The non-isomorphisms in each factor are given by the vanishing of the appropriate determinant, and the isomorphisms are just the elements of the general linear group G​l​(di,ℂ)Gl(d_{i},{\mathbb{C}}).

The cohomology of G​l​(n,ℂ)Gl(n,{\mathbb{C}}) is well understood and best expressed for our purposes in terms of the Poincaré polynomial.

Definition 7.13.

Let h0,…,hl,…h_{0},\ldots,h_{l},\ldots be the dimensions of the de Rham cohomology groups of a complex manifold TT. Then the Poincaré series (polynomial) PT​(q)P_{T}(q) is defined by

PT​(q)=∑i≥0hi​qi.P_{T}(q)=\sum_{i\geq 0}h_{i}q^{i}.

The Poincaré polynomial behaves very nicely under products M2=M1×M3M_{2}=M_{1}\times M_{3} of manifolds:

PM1​(q)⋅PM3​(q)=PM2​(q).P_{M_{1}}(q)\cdot P_{M_{3}}(q)=P_{M_{2}}(q).

An old result ([19], Theorems 7.11.A and 8.16.B) states that PG​l​(di,ℂ)​(q)=∏j=1di(1+t2​j−1)P_{Gl(d_{i},{\mathbb{C}})}(q)=\prod_{j=1}^{d_{i}}(1+t^{2j-1}). Hence the Poincaré polynomial of a product of general linear groups ∏i=1dPG​l​(di,ℂ)​(q)\prod_{i=1}^{d}P_{Gl(d_{i},{\mathbb{C}})}(q) equals

(11) ∏i=1d∏j=1di(1+t2​j−1)=(1+t)∑di>01⋅(1+t3)∑di>11⋅(1+t5)∑di>21⋅….\prod_{i=1}^{d}\prod_{j=1}^{d_{i}}(1+t^{2j-1})=(1+t)^{\sum_{d_{i}>0}1}\cdot(1+t^{3})^{\sum_{d_{i}>1}1}\cdot(1+t^{5})^{\sum_{d_{i}>2}1}\cdot\ldots.

Thus in order to compute the did_{i} one then has the following algorithm.

Algorithm 7.14.

Input: Generators and relations for the left module MM.

Output: The invariants did_{i} associated to EndD⁡(M)\operatorname{End}_{D}(M).

  1. (1)

    Compute the defect ideal Δ⁡(M)⊆K⁡[ν]\Delta(M)\subseteq K[\nu] by using Algorithm 7.9.

  2. (2)

    Compute the dimensions hk=dimℂ(Hd​Rk​(ℂn∖Var⁡(Δ⁡(M)))CLOSEh_{k}=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}(H^{k}_{dR}({\mathbb{C}}^{n}\setminus\operatorname{Var}(\Delta(M))).

  3. (3)

    Factor the polynomial PIsoD⁡(M)​(q):=∑hk​qkP_{\operatorname{Iso}_{D}(M)}(q):=\sum h_{k}q^{k} into

    (1+q)k1⋅(1+q3)k2⋅…⋅(1+q2​l−1)kl.(1+q)^{k_{1}}\cdot(1+q^{3})^{k_{2}}\cdot\ldots\cdot(1+q^{2l-1})^{k_{l}}.
  4. (4)

    Compute the did_{i} by comparing the expansion from the previous item with equation (11). Return the did_{i}.

Example 7.15.

Continuing our Example 7.11 we compute the de Rham cohomology groups of the complement of Var⁡(ν22​ν32+2​ν2​ν33+ν34+2​ν1​ν2​ν3​ν4+2​ν1​ν32​ν4+ν12​ν42)\operatorname{Var}(\nu_{2}^{2}\nu_{3}^{2}+2\nu_{2}\nu_{3}^{3}+\nu_{3}^{4}+2\nu_{1}\nu_{2}\nu_{3}\nu_{4}+2\nu_{1}\nu_{3}^{2}\nu_{4}+\nu_{1}^{2}\nu_{4}^{2}) in ℂ4{\mathbb{C}}^{4}. Using Macaulay2 one obtains h0=h1=h3=h4=1h_{0}=h_{1}=h_{3}=h_{4}=1 and all other hkh_{k} vanish. Then the Poincaré polynomial is 1+q+q3+q4=(1+q)​(1+q3)1+q+q^{3}+q^{4}=(1+q)(1+q^{3}). This means that d=1d=1 and d1=2d_{1}=2.

8. Appendix

In this section, we provide a short survey of the ideas that lead to an algorithm for restriction and then, mostly for purposes of reference here and otherwise, list an algorithm to compute integration. All the main ideas are taken from [10, 11, 16]

Definitions 8.1.

Fix an integer dd with 0≤d≤n0\leq d\leq n and set H=Var⁡(x1,…,xd)H=\operatorname{Var}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}). For α∈ℤn\alpha\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}, we set αH=(α1,…,αd,0,…,0)\alpha_{H}=(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{d},0,\ldots,0).

On the ring DD we define the VdV_{d}-filtration FHk​(D)F_{H}^{k}(D) as the KK-linear span of all operators xα∂βx^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta} for which |αH|+k≥|βH||\alpha_{H}|+k\geq|\beta_{H}|. More generally, on a free DD-module A=⊕j=1tD⋅ejA=\oplus_{j=1}^{t}D\cdot e_{j} we define

FHk​(A)​[𝔪]=∑j=1tFHk−𝔪⁡(j)​(D)⋅ej,F^{k}_{H}(A)[{\mathfrak{m}}]=\sum_{j=1}^{t}F^{k-{\mathfrak{m}}(j)}_{H}(D)\cdot e_{j},

where 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} is an element of ℤm{\mathbb{Z}}^{m}. We shall call 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} the shift vector. A shift vector is tied to a fixed set of generators.

We define the VdV_{d}-degree of an operator P∈A⁡[𝔪]P\in A[{\mathfrak{m}}], Vd​deg⁡(P⁡[𝔪])V_{d}\deg(P[{\mathfrak{m}}]), to be the smallest kk such that P∈FHk​(A⁡[𝔪])P\in F^{k}_{H}(A[{\mathfrak{m}}]).

If MM is a quotient of the free DD-module A=⊕1tD⋅ejA=\oplus_{1}^{t}D\cdot e_{j}, M=A/IM=A/I, we define the VdV_{d}-filtration on MM by FHk​(M⁡[𝔪])=FHk​(A⁡[𝔪])+IF^{k}_{H}(M[{\mathfrak{m}}])=F^{k}_{H}(A[{\mathfrak{m}}])+I. For submodules NN of AA we define the VdV_{d}-filtration by intersection: FHk​(N⁡[𝔪])=FHk​(A⁡[𝔪])∩NF^{k}_{H}(N[{\mathfrak{m}}])=F^{k}_{H}(A[{\mathfrak{m}}])\cap N.

If MM is a submodule of the free module A⁡[𝔪]A[{\mathfrak{m}}], then a VdV_{d}-strict Gröbner basis or a VdV_{d}-Gröbner basis for MM is a set of generators {m1,…,mτ}\{m_{1},\ldots,m_{\tau}\} for MM which satisfies: for all m∈Mm\in M we can find {αi}1τ∈D\{\alpha_{i}\}_{1}^{\tau}\in D such that m=∑αi​mim=\sum\alpha_{i}m_{i} and Vd​deg⁡(αi​mi​[𝔪])≤Vd​deg⁡(m⁡[𝔪])V_{d}\deg(\alpha_{i}m_{i}[{\mathfrak{m}}])\leq V_{d}\deg(m[{\mathfrak{m}}]) for all ii.

A complex of free DD-modules ⋯→Ai−1→ϕi−1Ai→ϕiAi+1→⋯\cdots\to A^{i-1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\phi^{i-1}}}{{\to}}A^{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\phi^{i}}}{{\to}}A^{i+1}\to\cdots is said to be VdV_{d}-adapted at AiA^{i} with respect to certain shift vectors 𝔪i−1,𝔪i,𝔪i+1{\mathfrak{m}}_{i-1},{\mathfrak{m}}_{i},{\mathfrak{m}}_{i+1} if

ϕi​(FHk​(Ai​[𝔪i]))⊆FHk​(Ai+1​[𝔪i+1])\phi^{i}\left(F^{k}_{H}(A^{i}[{\mathfrak{m}}_{i}])\right)\subseteq F^{k}_{H}(A^{i+1}[{\mathfrak{m}}_{i+1}])

and also

ϕi−1​(FHk​(Ai−1​[𝔪i−1]))⊆FHk​(Ai​[𝔪i])\phi^{i-1}\left(F^{k}_{H}(A^{i-1}[{\mathfrak{m}}_{i-1}])\right)\subseteq F^{k}_{H}(A^{i}[{\mathfrak{m}}_{i}])

for all kk.

im⁡(ϕi−1)∩FHk​(Ai​[𝔪i])=im⁡(ϕi−1|FHk​(Ai−1​[𝔪i−1]))\operatorname{im}(\phi^{i-1})\cap F^{k}_{H}(A^{i}[{\mathfrak{m}}_{i}])=\operatorname{im}(\phi^{i-1}|_{F^{k}_{H}(A^{i-1}[{\mathfrak{m}}_{i-1}])})

for all kk.

For 1≤d≤n1\leq d\leq n we set θd=x1∂1+…+xd∂d\theta_{d}=x_{1}\partial_{1}+\ldots+x_{d}\partial_{d} and θ0=0\theta_{0}=0. Recall that a DD-module M⁡[𝔪]=A⁡[𝔪]/IM[{\mathfrak{m}}]=A[{\mathfrak{m}}]/I is called specializable to HH if there is a polynomial b⁡(s)b(s) in a single variable such that

(12) b⁡(θd+k)⋅FHk​(M⁡[𝔪])\displaystyle b(\theta_{d}+k)\cdot F^{k}_{H}(M[{\mathfrak{m}}]) ⊆\displaystyle\subseteq FHk−1​(M⁡[𝔪])\displaystyle F^{k-1}_{H}(M[{\mathfrak{m}}])

b⁡(θd+k)⋅grHk⁡(M⁡[𝔪])=0.b(\theta_{d}+k)\cdot\operatorname{gr}^{k}_{H}(M[{\mathfrak{m}}])=0.

Remark 8.3.

Specializability descends to quotients and submodules. Namely, assume that M​[𝔪]=(A/I)​[𝔪]M[{\mathfrak{m}}]=(A/I)[{\mathfrak{m}}] is specializable and N⁡[𝔪]=(A′/I)​[𝔪]N[{\mathfrak{m}}]=(A^{\prime}/I)[{\mathfrak{m}}] is a submodule of MM (where I⊆A′⊆AI\subseteq A^{\prime}\subseteq A). Then clearly b⁡(θd+k)⋅FHk​(A⁡[𝔪])⊆FHk−1​(A⁡[𝔪])+A′b(\theta_{d}+k)\cdot F^{k}_{H}(A[{\mathfrak{m}}])\subseteq F^{k-1}_{H}(A[{\mathfrak{m}}])+A^{\prime} as well and hence (M/N)​[𝔪](M/N)[{\mathfrak{m}}] is specializable to HH. On the other hand, if P′∈FHk​(A′​[𝔪])=FHk​(A⁡[𝔪])∩A′P^{\prime}\in F^{k}_{H}(A^{\prime}[{\mathfrak{m}}])=F^{k}_{H}(A[{\mathfrak{m}}])\cap A^{\prime} then b⁡(θ+k)⋅P=Q+Q′b(\theta+k)\cdot P=Q+Q^{\prime} where Q∈FHk−1​(A⁡[𝔪])Q\in F^{k-1}_{H}(A[{\mathfrak{m}}]) and Q′∈IQ^{\prime}\in I and hence Q∈FHk−1​(A⁡[𝔪])∩A′=FHk​(A′​[𝔪])Q\in F^{k-1}_{H}(A[{\mathfrak{m}}])\cap A^{\prime}=F^{k}_{H}(A^{\prime}[{\mathfrak{m}}]). This implies that NN is also specializable and we see that the bb-functions for restriction of N⁡[𝔪]N[{\mathfrak{m}}] and for (M/N)​[𝔪](M/N)[{\mathfrak{m}}] divide the bb-function for restriction of M⁡[𝔪]M[{\mathfrak{m}}] to HH.

Notice that independently of dd, grH∙⁡(D⁡[0])≅D\operatorname{gr}^{\bullet}_{H}(D[0])\cong D, as a ring.

It has been shown by Oaku and Takayama in [10] (Proposition 3.8 and following remarks) how to compute VdV_{d}-strict Gröbner bases, and for any DD-module MM positioned in degree bb a free VdV_{d}-strict resolution (A∙​[𝔪∙],ϕ∙)(A^{\bullet}[{\mathfrak{m}}_{\bullet}],\phi^{\bullet}) of M⁡[𝔪b]M[{\mathfrak{m}}_{b}], Ai=⊕1riD,ri=0A^{i}=\oplus_{1}^{r_{i}}D,r_{i}=0 if i>bi>b. The construction given in [10] allows for arbitrary 𝔪b{\mathfrak{m}}_{b}.

The method employed is to construct a free resolution with the usual technique of finding a Gröbner basis for ker⁡(Ai→Ai+1)\ker(A^{i}\to A^{i+1}) and calculating the syzygies on this basis. The trick is to impose an order that refines the partial ordering given by VdV_{d}-degree, together with a homogenization technique.

In [16] was given an algorithm to compute VnV_{n}-strict resolutions for right bounded complexes, based on Eilenberg-MacLane resolutions. In [17] an improved algorithm is given that usually computes a much smaller resolution and is also easier to implement. We shall assume that the reader is familiar with the techniques from [10, 11, 16, 17].

An idea first stated in [11] and further developed in [16] yields a theorem which in order to state we need to introduce some more terminology for.

Definition 8.4.

Let Ω~d=D/{x1,…,xd}⋅D\tilde{\Omega}_{d}=D/\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}\}\cdot D and Ωd=D/{∂1,…,∂d}⋅D\Omega_{d}=D/\{\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{d}\}\cdot D.

The restriction of the complex A∙​[𝔪∙]A^{\bullet}[{\mathfrak{m}}_{\bullet}] to the subspace HH is the complex Ω~d⊗DLA∙​[𝔪∙]\tilde{\Omega}_{d}\otimes_{D}^{L}A^{\bullet}[{\mathfrak{m}}_{\bullet}] considered as a complex in the category of K⟨xd+1,∂d+1,…,xn,∂n⟩K\langle x_{d+1},\partial_{d+1},\ldots,x_{n},\partial_{n}\rangle-modules.

The integration of A∙​[𝔪∙]A^{\bullet}[{\mathfrak{m}}_{\bullet}] along HH is the complex Ωd⊗DLA∙​[𝔪∙]\Omega_{d}\otimes_{D}^{L}A^{\bullet}[{\mathfrak{m}}_{\bullet}] considered as a complex in that same category.

We need to make a convention about the VdV_{d}-filtration on tensor products over DD.

If A⁡[𝔪]A[{\mathfrak{m}}] is a free HH-graded DD-module with shift vector 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} then Ω~d⊗DA⁡[𝔪]\tilde{\Omega}_{d}\otimes_{D}A[{\mathfrak{m}}] is filtered by FHk​(Ω~d⊗DA⁡[𝔪]):=F^{k}_{H}(\tilde{\Omega}_{d}\otimes_{D}A[{\mathfrak{m}}]):= the KK-span of {P¯⊗DQ|Vd​deg⁡(P)+Vd​deg⁡(Q⁡[𝔪])≤k}\{\bar{P}\otimes_{D}Q|V_{d}\deg(P)+V_{d}\deg(Q[{\mathfrak{m}}])\leq k\}. Note that as Ω~d\tilde{\Omega}_{d} equals K[∂1,…,∂d]⟨xd+1,∂d+1,…,xn,∂n⟩K[\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{d}]\langle x_{d+1},\partial_{d+1},\ldots,x_{n},\partial_{n}\rangle as right DD-module, FHk​(Ω~d⊗DA⁡[𝔪])F^{k}_{H}(\tilde{\Omega}_{d}\otimes_{D}A[{\mathfrak{m}}]) equals the free K⟨xd+1,∂d+1,…,xn,∂n⟩K\langle x_{d+1},\partial_{d+1},\ldots,x_{n},\partial_{n}\rangle-module on the symbols {(P1,…,PrkD⁡(A))|Pj∈K[∂1,…,∂d],deg∂(Pj)≤k−𝔪(j)∀j}\{(P_{1},\ldots,P_{\operatorname{rk}_{D}(A)})|P_{j}\in K[\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{d}],\deg_{\partial}(P_{j})\leq k-{\mathfrak{m}}(j)\,\,\forall j\}.

If A∙​[𝔪∙]A^{\bullet}[{\mathfrak{m}}_{\bullet}] is a VdV_{d}-strict complex, we denote by FHk​(Ω~d⊗A∙​[𝔪∙])F^{k}_{H}(\tilde{\Omega}_{d}\otimes A^{\bullet}[{\mathfrak{m}}_{\bullet}]) the complex whose modules are the FHk​(Ω~d⊗Ai​[𝔪i])F^{k}_{H}(\tilde{\Omega}_{d}\otimes A^{i}[{\mathfrak{m}}_{i}]) as defined above, and the maps are induced from A∙A^{\bullet}.

Let us now consider the question how to compute Ωd⊗DLC∙\Omega_{d}\otimes_{D}^{L}C^{\bullet}. This problem is intimately related to the restriction algorithm. The reason is the Fourier transform, which is an algebra automorphism from DD to itself and defined as follows:

ℱd(xi)=∂i,ℱ(∂i)=−xi.{\mathcal{F}}_{d}(x_{i})=\partial_{i},\qquad{\mathcal{F}}(\partial_{i})=-x_{i}.

The perhaps surprising minus sign is required to keep the Leibniz relation xi∂i+1=∂ixix_{i}\partial_{i}+1=\partial_{i}x_{i} intact. The Fourier transform can be used to define an equivalence of the category of left DD-modules with itself via “extension of scalars”: ℱd​(M):=D⊗DM{\mathcal{F}}_{d}(M):=D\otimes_{D}M where DD is on the left considered as just DD while on the right DD acts on DD via ℱd{{\mathcal{F}}_{d}}. So for example if 1⊗m∈ℱd​(M)1\otimes m\in{\mathcal{F}}_{d}(M) then xi⋅1⊗m=xi⊗m=1⊗(−∂i⋅m)x_{i}\cdot 1\otimes m=x_{i}\otimes m=1\otimes(-\partial_{i}\cdot m).

If we apply ℱd{\mathcal{F}}_{d} to the integration problem we are reduced to computing the restriction of ℱd​(C∙){\mathcal{F}}_{d}(C^{\bullet}) since ℱd​(Ωd)=Ω~d{\mathcal{F}}_{d}(\Omega_{d})=\tilde{\Omega}_{d}. We are led to introduce therefore a V~d\tilde{V}_{d}-filtration which is defined by
